cards.explanation: The answer is maidens. She says, "No wonder the maidens adore you." The way I read it, his name is so well loved that the compliments show up before he does. That's a man whose cologne gets complimented before he's even parked the car.

The answer is the king. She says, "May the king bring me to his chambers." Notice she asks it in the same breath as "Take me away with you…" She's not asking for a map, friends. She's asking to be taken.

The answer is True. After all those "I" lines, the song says, "we will praise your love more than wine." It's like the whole room just joined the chorus. Funny how a solo can turn into a group number in half a verse.

The answer is the sun. She says, "Do not stare because I am dark, for the sun has gazed upon me." The sun gets the credit, and she asks them not to stare. I think she's saying, "Okay, ladies, show's over."
The answer is vineyards. She says, "they made me a keeper of the vineyards…" Her mother's sons were angry with her, and that's the job they gave her. I think that's a lot of rows to look after.

The answer is that she doesn't want to be like a veiled woman by his companions' flocks. She asks, "Why should I be like a veiled woman beside the flocks of your companions?" She wants to find him instead of standing by somebody else's sheep. I think she's tired of guessing which flock is his.
The answer is shepherds. The reply comes back, "…graze your young goats near the tents of the shepherds." Follow the flock, find the tents. Sounds like a good plan for a girl with goats.

The answer is False. He says, "I compare you, my darling, to a mare among Pharaoh’s chariots." The text gives him warm words for her, calling her "my darling" and then going on about her cheeks and neck. Nobody here is teasing, friends.

The answer is gold studded with silver beads. The verse says, "We will make you ornaments of gold, studded with beads of silver." It's a promise, and it's a shiny one. The "we" is back with something to say to her.

The answer is her perfume. She says, "While the king was at his table, my perfume spread its fragrance." The king is at his table, and her perfume is spreading its fragrance. I'd say she's getting noticed.

The answer is True. She says, "My beloved is to me a cluster of henna blossoms in the vineyards of En-gedi." That's another picture for him, right after the sachet of myrrh. She's running out of ways to say it and not out of love.

The answer is handsome. She says, "How handsome you are, my beloved! Oh, how delightful!" He said beautiful, and she throws it right back to him. Nobody is leaving this conversation without a compliment.
The answer is False. She says, "The beams of our house are cedars; our rafters are fragrant firs." Cedar beams and fir rafters, both fragrant woods. Gold is back in verse 11, as ornaments for her.

The answer is that she stands out from all the rest. He says, "Like a lily among the thorns is my darling among the maidens." Thorns on one side and a lily on the other makes it easy to see who stands out. The picture puts her up against the other maidens, and she's the lily.

The answer is shade. She says, "I delight to sit in his shade, and his fruit is sweet to my taste." An apple tree gives you shade and fruit, and that's two gifts for one tree. I'd sit there too, friends.

The answer is that she is faint with love. She asks, "Sustain me with raisins; refresh me with apples, for I am faint with love." The text gives us the reason right there in her own words. I think she's got it bad.
The answer is False. She says, "Do not arouse or awaken love until the time is right." She doesn't tell them to rush anything. The timing matters to her, and she asks them to respect that.
